prompt: A closed system can exchange:
options: neither matter nor energy with its surroundings
both matter and energy with its surroundings
energy but not matter with its surroundings
matter but not energy with its surroundings
why: A closed system (e.g. a sealed flask) lets heat in or out but no substances can enter or leave.

prompt: A dish of water left uncovered eventually dries out, but water in a sealed jar keeps a constant level. The main reason is that
options: water does not evaporate in a sealed jar
the sealed jar is an open system
the air in the jar absorbs the water vapour permanently
in the sealed jar the vapour cannot escape, so condensation can balance evaporation
why: Only in a closed system can the vapour stay and condense back, letting the two opposing processes balance.

prompt: Calcium carbonate is heated strongly in an open crucible. It decomposes completely to calcium oxide. Why does it not reach equilibrium?
options: the forward rate is too slow
CO₂ escapes from the open system, so the reverse reaction cannot occur
why: With CO₂ lost to the air there is nothing for CaO to react with, so the reaction goes to completion.

prompt: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate turns white when heated, and turns blue again when water is added to the white powder. This shows that
options: copper(II) sulfate is an open system
the system is at static equilibrium
why: Both directions can be made to happen: water is removed on heating and taken back up when added.

prompt: For a chemical system to reach equilibrium, it must be
options: a non-reversible reaction in a closed system
an exothermic reaction in an open system
any reaction at a constant temperature
a reversible reaction in a closed system
why: Both conditions are needed: products must be able to re-form reactants, and nothing may escape.

prompt: Which change is reversible under ordinary laboratory conditions?
options: Dissolving iodine crystals in water until the solution is saturated
why: Dissolving and crystallising are opposite processes that both occur; the others form products that cannot re-form the reactants.

prompt: An opened bottle of soft drink slowly goes flat, but a sealed bottle stays fizzy. Which statement is correct?
options: The opened bottle is a closed system that has reached equilibrium
The sealed bottle is a closed system where CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) can reach equilibrium
CO₂ stops dissolving once the bottle is sealed
The sealed bottle is an open system because it can be warmed
why: Sealed, CO₂ gas above the liquid stays and dissolves as fast as it leaves; opened, CO₂ escapes, so the system is open.

prompt: The combustion of methane is treated as non-reversible mainly because
options: combustion is always done in a closed system
the reverse reaction is extremely unfavourable, as the forward reaction is very exothermic and products are stable
the reaction has a very low activation energy
why: Re-forming methane and oxygen from CO₂ and water would need a huge input of energy, so it does not happen to any measurable extent.

prompt: A student says: "Burning ethanol in a sealed bomb calorimeter will reach equilibrium because the system is closed." What is wrong with this statement?
options: A bomb calorimeter is an open system
Ethanol cannot burn in a sealed container
Being closed is not enough; combustion is not reversible under these conditions
why: A closed system is necessary but not sufficient; the reaction must also be reversible.

prompt: Which is an example of an open system?
options: A beaker of hydrochloric acid reacting with zinc, with no lid
A stoppered flask of saturated salt solution
A sealed syringe of NO₂ and N₂O₄
A sealed glass tube containing iodine crystals and vapour
why: Hydrogen gas escapes from the open beaker, so matter leaves the system.

prompt: The colour of a sealed mixture of Fe³⁺ and SCN⁻ ions can be made darker and then lighter again many times by changing conditions. This is evidence that
options: the mixture is an open system
the reaction has gone to completion
the reaction forming FeSCN²⁺ is reversible
why: Shifting back and forth in both directions is only possible if the reaction runs both ways.

prompt: Cooking an egg is non-reversible because
options: the egg is a closed system
the proteins are permanently denatured and cannot re-form their original structure on cooling
why: Cooling the egg does not restore the original protein shapes, so the change cannot be reversed.

prompt: Which pair describes the system in a sealed flask containing N₂O₄ and NO₂ gases?
why: The gases cannot escape, and N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ runs in both directions.

prompt: Pink hydrated cobalt(II) chloride turns blue on heating and pink again in moist air. If the blue paper is sealed in a dry, airtight container it stays blue. This is because
options: no water can reach it, so the reverse (hydration) reaction cannot occur
the container is an open system
the blue form cannot react with water
why: The reverse reaction needs water; in a dry closed container there is none available.

prompt: A reaction is described as "non-reversible" when
options: it happens in an open system
the products cannot re-form the reactants to any significant extent under the conditions used
why: Non-reversible means the reverse reaction is negligible, so it goes essentially to completion.

prompt: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are not an equilibrium system inside a plant because
options: they are different reactions, at different times and places and with different energy sources, not one reaction in a closed system
why: Overall equations are opposite, but they are separate processes in an open system, not the forward and reverse of one equilibrium.

prompt: At equilibrium, the concentrations of the reactants and products are
options: zero, because the reaction has stopped
why: Equal forward and reverse rates keep each concentration constant; the values themselves are usually different.

prompt: A student writes: "At equilibrium the reaction stops." Which correction is right?
options: The forward reaction stops but the reverse continues
Both reactions continue, at equal rates, so there is no overall change
The reverse reaction stops but the forward continues
The reaction stops only when K = 1
why: Equilibrium in chemistry is dynamic: particles keep reacting in both directions.

prompt: As a reaction approaches equilibrium starting from pure reactants, the rate of the reverse reaction
options: stays at zero until equilibrium is reached
is always equal to the forward rate
starts at zero and increases until it equals the forward rate
why: There are no products at first, so the reverse rate is zero; it rises as products build up.

prompt: Using collision theory, the forward rate falls as a reaction approaches equilibrium because
options: the temperature falls as the reaction proceeds
reactant concentrations fall, so there are fewer collisions per second between reactant particles
the products block the reactant particles
why: Rate depends on collision frequency, which falls as the reactants are used up.

prompt: Some deuterium gas (D₂) is added to an equilibrium mixture of N₂, H₂ and NH₃. Soon NH₂D and similar molecules are detected. This shows that
options: the equilibrium is dynamic: NH₃ is still being formed and decomposed
the reaction had gone to completion
why: Deuterium can only end up in ammonia if ammonia is still forming (and breaking down) at equilibrium.

prompt: One flask starts with pure N₂O₄ and an identical flask starts with the equivalent amount of pure NO₂, at the same temperature. At equilibrium
options: both flasks contain the same equilibrium mixture
the first flask contains only NO₂
the second flask contains only N₂O₄
the flasks contain different mixtures that never become the same
why: Equilibrium can be approached from either direction and gives the same position under the same conditions.

prompt: On a concentration–time graph, equilibrium has been reached when
options: all the concentration lines have become horizontal
the reactant and product lines cross
the product line reaches its highest gradient
why: Constant concentrations show the forward and reverse rates are equal.

prompt: On a rate–time graph for a reversible reaction started with reactants only, the forward and reverse rate lines
options: cross and continue in opposite directions
meet and then stay together as a single horizontal line
why: At equilibrium the two rates are equal and constant.

prompt: A saturated sodium chloride solution sits in a sealed flask with undissolved crystals. The mass of crystals stays constant because
options: dissolving and crystallising continue at equal rates
no more salt can dissolve at all
why: This is a dynamic solution equilibrium: NaCl(s) ⇌ Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).

prompt: Which observation would NOT be expected for a system at equilibrium in a sealed container?
options: The colour of the mixture slowly keeps getting darker
why: Any steady change in a macroscopic property shows the system is not yet at equilibrium.

prompt: Increasing the temperature increases the rate of a reaction mainly because
options: a larger fraction of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy
why: Higher temperature shifts the energy distribution so more collisions are successful.

prompt: A static equilibrium differs from a dynamic equilibrium because in a static equilibrium
options: the forward and reverse rates are equal and non-zero
the forward and reverse processes have both stopped
why: Static means no processes occur at all; in dynamic equilibrium both continue at equal rates.

prompt: For a successful collision between reactant particles, the particles must
options: be in the same phase as a catalyst
collide with at least the activation energy and in a suitable orientation
collide with less than the activation energy
collide with any energy as long as they are in the gas phase
why: Both enough energy and correct orientation are needed for bonds to break and new ones to form.

prompt: In the equilibrium H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), the purple colour stays constant once equilibrium is reached because
options: I₂ is used up by the forward reaction exactly as fast as it is made by the reverse reaction
why: Equal rates mean [I₂] does not change, so the colour is constant.

prompt: Radioactive ¹⁴CO₂ is bubbled into a sealed container holding CaCO₃(s), CaO(s) and CO₂(g) at equilibrium at a high temperature. Later, some of the solid CaCO₃ is found to be radioactive. This shows
options: CaO and CO₂ are still reacting to form CaCO₃ at equilibrium
why: The labelled carbon can only get into the solid if the reverse reaction is still happening.

prompt: Argon gas is added to the equilibrium N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at constant volume. The equilibrium position
options: does not change, because the partial concentrations of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ are unchanged
shifts right, because argon is a catalyst
shifts right, because the total pressure increased
shifts left, because argon dilutes the gases
why: Total pressure rises, but the concentrations of the reacting gases (and so Q) stay the same.

prompt: The volume of a container holding H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) at equilibrium is halved. The purple colour
options: becomes darker, because [I₂] doubles, but the equilibrium position does not shift
becomes paler, because the equilibrium shifts right
becomes darker, because the equilibrium shifts left
why: There are 2 mol of gas on each side, so no shift occurs; the colour darkens only because the gas is more concentrated.

prompt: The volume of a container holding 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) is suddenly decreased at constant temperature. The brown colour
options: darkens immediately, then fades partly as the equilibrium shifts right
darkens and stays dark with no further change
why: Compressing raises [NO₂] at once; the system then shifts to the side with fewer gas molecules (N₂O₄), partly reducing the colour.

prompt: For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), the volume of the container is decreased. The equilibrium
options: shifts left, because only CO₂ is a gas and the left has fewer gas molecules
does not shift, because there are solids on both sides
shifts right, because the pressure increased
shifts right, because there are more particles on the right
why: Count only gas molecules: 0 on the left and 1 on the right, so the system shifts left to lower the pressure.

prompt: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at equilibrium, at t = 5 min the [N₂] line jumps up suddenly and then slowly decreases, the [H₂] line slowly decreases and the [NH₃] line slowly increases. What change was made at t = 5 min?
why: Only N₂ jumps, so N₂ was added; the system shifts right to use some of it up.

prompt: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at equilibrium, at t = 8 min all three concentration lines jump up instantly by the same factor; then [NH₃] rises further while [N₂] and [H₂] fall. What change was made?
options: The volume of the container was decreased
why: All concentrations jumping by the same factor means compression; the shift right reduces the number of gas molecules.

prompt: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) (ΔH positive) at equilibrium, at t = 4 min no line jumps, but [NO₂] gradually increases and [N₂O₄] gradually decreases to new constant values. What change was made?
why: A gradual change with no jump is a temperature change; the shift towards NO₂ is the endothermic direction, so it was heated.

prompt: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at equilibrium, at t = 6 min the [NH₃] line drops suddenly, then [NH₃] slowly rises while [N₂] and [H₂] slowly fall. What change was made?
why: A sudden drop in one line only means that species was removed; the system shifts right to replace some of it.

prompt: Two identical experiments are run, one with a catalyst. On the concentration–time graphs, the lines for the catalysed reaction
options: become horizontal at higher product concentrations
become horizontal later, at lower product concentrations
become horizontal sooner, but at the same final concentrations
why: A catalyst speeds up reaching equilibrium without changing the equilibrium concentrations.

prompt: On a concentration–time graph for a reaction that starts with only A, [A] falls by 0.40 mol L⁻¹ while [B] rises by 0.80 mol L⁻¹ before both lines level off. Which equation fits this graph?
why: B changes twice as much as A, so the mole ratio is 1 : 2.

prompt: On a concentration–time graph, the steepness (gradient) of a concentration line at a given time represents
options: the rate at which that species is being formed or used up
why: Gradient = change in concentration per unit time, which is a rate.

prompt: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) (ΔH negative) at equilibrium, at t = 10 min no line jumps, but [SO₃] gradually falls and [SO₂] and [O₂] gradually rise. Which change was made?
why: No jump means a temperature change; the shift to the left is the endothermic direction, so the mixture was heated.

prompt: Immediately after extra N₂ is added to the equilibrium N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), the reaction quotient Q is
options: less than K, so the forward reaction is favoured until Q = K
equal to K, so nothing happens
greater than K, so the forward reaction is favoured
greater than K, so the reverse reaction is favoured
why: N₂ is in the denominator of Q, so adding it lowers Q below K.

prompt: An equilibrium mixture is heated. Immediately afterwards, before any concentrations change, which statement is correct?
options: Q has changed, but K has not
Both Q and K are unchanged
K has changed, but Q has not, so Q no longer equals K
